Table row: Manual snapshots (Standard and Enterprise Editions) 5 per AWS Managed Microsoft AD; Service Quotas page: manual snapshots 5, Adjustable No.

What's New (Aug 15, 2025) supports Standard 5->25 and Enterprise 125->500 accounts, but the quoted rows say 'Shared domains', and the Hybrid 125 as an account count rests on footnote *** ('number of accounts that an individual directory can be shared to') which is not in the evidence; also adjustable=false is unsupported by its own admission.
Simple AD quotas: directories 10 (default, per Region), manual snapshots 5 per Simple AD; Service Quotas page: Simple AD directories 10, Adjustable Yes.
AD Connector compatibility note states verbatim: Amazon RDS is compatible with AWS Managed Microsoft AD only, and is not compatible with AD Connector.
FAQ: seamless join is at launch and from the console; cannot be used from the console for existing instances, which can be joined via the EC2 API or PowerShell on the instance.

Sharing page: share a single directory with trusted accounts in the same organization or accounts outside it; the shared directory in the consumer account holds metadata enabling EC2 seamless domain join.
Considerations > Pricing: AWS charges an additional fee for directory sharing; the account using the shared directory is the account charged the sharing fees.
Sharing methods: Organizations needs All features and the directory in the management account and does not require consumers to accept; handshake requires the consumer account to accept.
Network connectivity is a prerequisite for cross-account sharing; VPC peering, Transit Gateway and VPN are named as examples ('some of these include').
Important Notice verbatim: no longer open to new customers; for similar capabilities explore AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector.
Availability-change note: only new onboarding is not permitted; existing customers retain full functionality, are not affected and can continue to create new Simple AD directories.
What-is page: AD-compatible, powered by Samba 4, supports user accounts, group memberships, joining Linux/Windows EC2 instances, Kerberos-based SSO and group policies.

Simple AD page: standalone managed directory powered by Samba 4, a subset of Managed AD features; does not support MFA, trusts, PowerShell, recycle bin, gMSA, schema extensions for POSIX and Microsoft apps (claim omits only ADAC).
Two sizes: Small up to 500 users (approximately 2,000 objects), Large up to 5,000 users (approximately 20,000 objects); 'about' matches 'approximately'.

What-is page lists exactly MFA, trusts, DNS dynamic update, schema extensions, LDAPS, PowerShell AD cmdlets, FSMO role transfer; not compatible with RDS SQL Server; use Managed AD for actual Microsoft AD.
Quotas page: generally, no more than 500 users in Small and 5,000 in Large; 'advises' matches 'Generally, you should not'.
When to use: standalone directory for Windows workloads needing basic AD features, compatible AWS applications, or Linux workloads needing LDAP service.
Trust prerequisites: first connect the self-managed network to the VPC with Managed AD, both firewalls open the listed AD ports; set up DNS conditional forwarders on the self-managed domain.
Trust page: one and two-way external and forest trusts with self-managed directories and between Managed AD directories; all three directions Incoming, Outgoing, Two-way.

Two-way trust required for AWS Enterprise Apps incl. Quick, IAM Identity Center, WorkMail, WorkSpaces, console, as Managed AD must query self-managed users and groups; EC2, RDS, FSx work with one- or two-way.
What-is page: multiple ways to use Microsoft AD with other AWS services; multiple directory choices for existing Microsoft AD or LDAP-aware applications in the cloud.

Which-to-choose row matches each recommendation: Standard/Enterprise for actual AD or LDAP for Linux, Hybrid to extend self-managed AD, AD Connector for on-prem login and EC2 join, Simple AD low-scale low-cost.

The row supports 'use Amazon Cognito' for high-scale SaaS with subscribers and social identities, but it sits under 'Recommended AWS Directory Service options' and nowhere says 'not a Directory Service directory'; that contrast is added by the claim.
Attributes for access control: selected attributes from the identity source are passed to the accessed account as session tags referenced with aws:PrincipalTag/{tag-key}.

ABAC page: attributes from any identity source are called tags, users get access only to resources with matching tags; same permission set example and access changes via the directory without permission updates in AWS.
IdP can send attributes as session tags through SAML assertions; an ABAC mapping for the same attribute on the page takes precedence and replaces the IdP value.
Instances page: bound to a single account, visible only within that account and Region; What-is page: use account instances only for isolated deployments of select AWS managed applications.

Quotes give the admin-permits condition (after Nov 15, 2023) and manual enablement (before), but the claim drops the further required conditions (no blocking SCP, no existing instance in the account, supported Region) and its wording reads as if the admin permits by default, which the quote does not say.
Account instances page: limited to one account instance per AWS account; used only for supported applications in the same account and Region.
Resiliency page: not recommended for resiliency because they do not support AWS account access and create a second, isolated control point not connected to the organization instance.
Resiliency page verbatim: access determined from the enabled Region, AWS accounts are global, users can operate in any Region when accessing accounts through Identity Center.
FAQ: add any AWS account managed using AWS Organizations; need to enable all features to manage account single sign-on.
Considerations for AD Connector: access only to users and groups of the single attached domain; password resets must be done within AD, not from the AWS access portal.
Considerations: AD Connector or Managed AD directory must reside in the Organizations management account, or in the delegated admin account when delegated admin is enabled.
Pass-through authentication to the source AD via Directory Service; user, group and membership info synced, no password information because authentication happens in the source directory.
Microsoft AD directory page: connect a self-managed AD or a Managed AD directory via Directory Service; with Managed AD as source, users from any domain connected through an AD trust.
Administrator-initiated: admins can end a user's session; works as if users signed out themselves, requiring them to sign in again.
